title: It's All Connected: A Journey Through Test-Time Memorization, Attentional Bias, Retention, and Online Optimization
authors: Ali Behrouz, Meisam Razaviyayn, Peilin Zhong, Vahab Mirrokni (Google Research)
tldr: This is the 'grand unifying theory' paper of the test-time-training line: it re-derives Transformers, all modern linear RNNs (RetNet, Mamba2, GLA, DeltaNet, Gated DeltaNet, RWKV-7, Longhorn, TTT, Titans), and softmax attention itself as associative-memory modules that minimize an internal objective -- which the authors name the 'attentional bias' -- online over the key/value stream. It shows that essentially every existing model uses one of only two attentional biases (dot-product similarity or L2 regression) and one retention mechanism (L2 regularization, which is what a 'forget gate' really is), then opens up the design space along four axes: memory architecture, attentional-bias objective, retention gate, and memory-learning algorithm (the Miras framework). Three new instantiations -- Moneta (Lp loss + Lq-norm retention), Yaad (Huber loss), Memora (L2 loss + KL-divergence retention over a probability simplex, i.e., a softmax-normalized memory) -- each with a 2-layer-MLP memory trained by chunkwise-parallel gradient descent, outperform Transformer++, Gated DeltaNet, Samba, and Titans-era baselines at up to 1.3B params / 100B tokens on language modeling, commonsense reasoning, and RULER needle-in-haystack.
problem_and_motivation: Transformers dominate sequence modeling but pay quadratic time and a linearly growing KV cache, which caps long-context applicability. The efficient-recurrent alternatives (linear attention, RetNet, Mamba/Mamba2, GLA, DeltaNet and its gated variants, RWKV, TTT, Titans) compress the context into a fixed-size state, and the field has been improving them along three empirical fronts: better learning rules (Hebbian -> delta rule -> momentum/deep-memory rules), better forget gates (LSTM -> Mamba2 -> Titans), and more expressive memory structures (vector -> matrix -> deep MLP). But there was no single design framework that explains WHY these choices work, unifies all of them (prior unifying attempts -- Mamba2's SSD framework, Longhorn's online-learning view, Sun et al.'s TTT regression view, and the concurrent Wang et al. 2025 'test-time regression' framework -- each cover only a subset, cannot express forget gates cleanly, or force all models into a single regression objective, erasing real distinctions such as Hebbian-vs-delta updates). The paper's motivating question is: what is the underlying design framework behind these sequence models, and how can models be systematically enhanced beyond the two objectives (dot-product, L2) and one regularizer (L2) that everyone implicitly uses? The cognitive-science framing is 'attentional bias': human memory prioritizes certain stimuli; the internal objective of a sequence model is exactly its bias about what to prioritize when memorizing. A second motivation is reinterpreting forgetting: the paper argues models never truly erase memory -- gates are better understood as RETENTION regularizers that trade off learning new associations against staying close to (retaining) the previous state, mirroring the neuroscience view that memories become inaccessible via retrieval failure rather than erasure.
core_mechanism:
=== 1. Associative memory and attentional bias (Definition 3.1) ===
An associative memory is an operator $\mathcal{M}: \mathcal{K} \to \mathcal{V}$ mapping keys $\mathbf{k} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_k}$ to values $\mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_v}$ (keys/values are linear projections of the input token $x_t$, exactly as in attention). Learning the mapping means solving
$$\mathcal{M}^* = \arg\min_{\mathcal{M}} \; L(\mathcal{M}(K); V),$$
where the objective $L$ is called the ATTENTIONAL BIAS: it defines what the memory considers a good recall and therefore which events it prioritizes. When the memory is parameterized by weights $W$ (a vector, matrix, or MLP), the optimization is over $W$, optionally with a regularizer $R(W)$ controlling retention of past data. Crucially (Remark 2) this is a meta-learning / bilevel problem: the attentional bias is optimized in the INNER loop (at test time, per token), while all other network parameters (projections, convolutions, gate-producing layers) are optimized in the OUTER loop by ordinary pre-training. Shorthand used throughout: $\ell(W_{t-1};\mathbf{k}_t,\mathbf{v}_t) := L(\mathcal{M}(W;\mathbf{k}_t), \mathbf{v}_t)$.

The base inner update is one step of online gradient descent:
$$W_t = W_{t-1} - \eta_t \nabla \ell(W_{t-1}; \mathbf{k}_t, \mathbf{v}_t),$$
with $\eta_t$ a (possibly data-dependent, channel-wise) inner learning rate. Titans read this same quantity as a 'momentary surprise' signal; here it is just online GD on the attentional bias.

=== 2. Two optimization viewpoints (the theoretical spine) ===
(FTRL Viewpoint) Online GD is a special case of Follow-The-Regularized-Leader. With $W_0=0$, the GD step equals
$$W_t = \arg\min_{W \in \mathcal{W}} \sum_{i=1}^{t} \hat{\ell}_i(W;\mathbf{k}_i,\mathbf{v}_i) + \tfrac{1}{\eta_t} R_t(W),$$
where in the classical case $\hat{\ell}_i(W) = \langle W - W_{i-1}, \nabla\ell(W_{i-1};\mathbf{k}_i,\mathbf{v}_i)\rangle$ (a local linearization of the loss at each past step) and $R_t(W)=\tfrac{1}{2}\|W\|_2^2$. The sum term memorizes ALL past tokens; $R_t$ penalizes memory magnitude ('memory stability'). Generalizing $\hat{\ell}_i$ and $R_t$ yields mirror-descent-type algorithms.

(Learning-Retaining Viewpoint) Alternatively, the same GD step is
$$W_t = \arg\min_{W \in \mathcal{W}} \tilde{\ell}_t(W;\mathbf{k}_t,\mathbf{v}_t) + \mathrm{Ret}_t(W, W_{t-1}),$$
i.e., fit the LATEST pair while staying close to the previous state. The retention term decomposes into local and global parts:
$$\mathrm{Ret}_t(W,W_{t-1}) = \tfrac{1}{\eta_t}\, D_t(W, W_{t-1}) \;+\; \tfrac{1}{\alpha_t}\, G_t(W),$$
where $D_t$ is a premetric penalizing deviation from $W_{t-1}$ (local retention; $\eta_t$ acts as a 'meta in-context learning rate' -- large $\eta_t$ = learn more, forget more), and $G_t$ penalizes memory size globally (global retention; this is where classical forget gates live). Proposition 3.2 (proved in Appendix B by induction): if $\eta_t=\eta$, $\mathcal{W}=\mathbb{R}^d$, and one sets $\mathrm{Ret}_t = D_h(W,W')$, the Bregman divergence of $h_t(W) := \sum_{i=1}^{t-1}\hat{\ell}_i(W) + \tfrac{1}{\eta}R(W)$ (assumed strictly convex), then Learning-Retaining reproduces FTRL exactly. Hence Learning-Retaining is the more general lens and the paper derives everything from it. Remark 3: under this lens there is no 'forgetting' -- the model merely declines to retain; hence the renaming of forget gate to RETENTION GATE. Remark 4: the definition is optimizer-agnostic -- Newton's method (Mesa-layer) and non-parametric solutions (softmax attention) also fit.

=== 3. Miras: the four design choices ===
1. Memory architecture: vector, matrix ($\mathcal{M}(W,\mathbf{k})=W\mathbf{k}$), MLP, or richer; optionally constrained ($W$ in an L2 ball, or a scaled probability simplex).
2. Attentional bias: the objective $L$ (or its approximation $\hat\ell/\tilde\ell$). Determines how the memory maps inputs and prioritizes events.
3. Retention gate: $R_t$ (FTRL) or $\mathrm{Ret}_t$ (Learning-Retaining). Balances plasticity vs. stability; the paper claims this is the key lever for long-context performance.
4. Memory learning algorithm: GD, GD+momentum, implicit GD, Newton, multi-step GD, or closed-form/non-parametric solutions.
Minor axes: data-dependent vs. independent gates, scalar vs. channel-wise parameters.

=== 4. How existing models fall out (the unification, Table 1) ===
- Hebbian family (LA, RetNet, Lightning Attention, Mamba2, GLA): attentional bias = dot-product similarity $\tilde\ell_t = -2\langle \mathcal{M}_t \mathbf{k}_t, \mathbf{v}_t\rangle$; local retention $\mathrm{Ret}_t = \|\mathcal{M}_t - \alpha \mathcal{M}_{t-1}\|_F^2$; GD gives
$$\mathcal{M}_t = \alpha \mathcal{M}_{t-1} + \mathbf{v}_t \mathbf{k}_t^{\top}.$$
$\alpha=1$: linear attention. Learnable scalar $\alpha$: RetNet ($n{=}1$ vector state) / Lightning Attention ($n{>}1$). Data-dependent $\alpha_t$: Mamba2. (GLA: diagonal $\mathrm{Diag}(\alpha_t)$; HGRN2 uses an L1-style bias with tied write $\mathbf{v}_t(1-\alpha_t)^\top$.)
- Delta-rule family (DeltaNet, Longhorn, Gated DeltaNet, RWKV-7): attentional bias = L2 regression $\|\mathcal{M}_t\mathbf{k}_t - \mathbf{v}_t\|_2^2$, same Frobenius local retention, (stochastic) GD:
$$\mathcal{M}_t = \alpha\,(I - \eta_t \mathbf{k}_t\mathbf{k}_t^{\top})\,\mathcal{M}_{t-1} + \mathbf{v}_t\mathbf{k}_t^{\top}.$$
$\alpha=1$: DeltaNet. Data-dependent scalar $\alpha_t$: Gated DeltaNet; channel-wise vector ($m=d$): RWKV-7. Longhorn = same objective solved by IMPLICIT gradient descent (closed-form proximal step). DeltaProduct = multiple GD steps per token (product of Householders).
- Beyond delta: Titans-LMM = NONLINEAR L2 bias $\|\mathcal{M}_t(\mathbf{k}_t)-\mathbf{v}_t\|_2^2$ (deep MLP memory) with BOTH local $D_t=\|W_t-W_{t-1}\|_F^2$ and global $G_t=\|W_t\|_2^2$ retention, optimized by GD WITH MOMENTUM: $\mathcal{M}_t = \alpha_t\mathcal{M}_{t-1} - S_t$, $S_t = \eta_t S_{t-1} - \theta_t\nabla\ell(\mathcal{M}_{t-1};\mathbf{k}_t,\mathbf{v}_t)$. (Footnote: Titans' gate differs from Mamba2/GDN gating in the full-erase limit -- Titans 'cold-starts' by still using the previous memory to score surprise before erasing.) TTT-Linear/TTT-MLP = same L2 bias, GD, no retention gate. Mesa-layer = full-history objective $\sum_{i=1}^{t}\|\mathcal{M}_t(\mathbf{k}_i)-\mathbf{v}_i\|_2^2 + \|\mathcal{M}_t\|_2^2$ solved by Newton's method.
- Softmax attention = the NON-PARAMETRIC Nadaraya-Watson estimator solution of the L2 regression loss, with no retention (memory = the growing set $\{(\mathbf{k}_t,\mathbf{v}_t)\}$, i.e., the KV cache). This is why attention has perfect recall and linear state growth: it never compresses.

=== 5. New attentional biases (Section 5.1) ===
(a) $\ell_p$ bias: $L = \|\mathcal{M}(\mathbf{k}_t)-\mathbf{v}_t\|_p^p$, $p\ge 1$. For matrix memory the GD step is
$$W_t = W_{t-1} - p\,\eta_t\,\big[\mathrm{Sign}(W\mathbf{k}_t-\mathbf{v}_t)\odot|W\mathbf{k}_t-\mathbf{v}_t|^{p-1}\big]\mathbf{k}_t^{\top}.$$
$p$ tunes noise sensitivity ($p{<}2$ robust, $p{>}2$ accentuates large errors). At $p=1$: $W_t = W_{t-1} - \eta_t\,\mathrm{Sign}(W_t\mathbf{k}_t-\mathbf{v}_t)\,\mathbf{k}_t^{\top}$ -- a 'value-less associative memory' that stores which keys occurred but maps them only to $\pm 1$ (analogy: human coping, not storing values of extreme events). Because Sign and $|\cdot|$ break backprop, they are smoothed: $\mathrm{Sign}(x)\approx\tanh(\alpha x)$, $|x| \approx \sqrt{x^2+\epsilon}$ ($\epsilon=10^{-6}$) -- essential for OUTER-loop training stability.
(b) Huber bias (robust memory / 'coping mechanism'), three forms: (i) coordinate-wise Huber $\ell = \sum_j \mathcal{H}(\mathcal{M}(W,\mathbf{k}_t)_j - v_{t,j})$ with $\mathcal{H}(a)=\tfrac12 a^2$ if $|a|\le\delta$, else $\delta|a|-\tfrac12\delta^2$; the update mixes the L2 gradient on in-threshold coordinates with a sign (value-less) gradient on outlier coordinates, selected by the indicator mask $\mathbb{I}(|W\mathbf{k}_t-\mathbf{v}_t|\le\delta_t)$; (ii) Huber of the residual norm $\ell=\mathcal{H}(\|\mathcal{M}(W,\mathbf{k}_t)-\mathbf{v}_t\|_2)$, whose GD step uses the raw residual outer product when $\|\cdot\|\le\delta_t$ and the NORMALIZED residual direction times $\delta_t$ otherwise (a per-token gradient clip); (iii) smooth mixture -- the form actually used in Yaad:
$$W_t = W_{t-1} - \begin{cases}\eta_t\,\nabla\ell_2(W_{t-1};\mathbf{k}_t,\mathbf{v}_t) & \text{if } \|\mathcal{M}(\mathbf{k}_t)-\mathbf{v}_t\| \le \delta_t,\\ \eta_t\,\delta_t\,\nabla\ell_1(W_{t-1};\mathbf{k}_t,\mathbf{v}_t) & \text{otherwise.}\end{cases}$$
$\delta_t$ is input-dependent and learned: the memory itself decides per token whether an event is an outlier whose magnitude should be discounted.
(c) Robust-to-value-shift bias: worst-case loss $L=\max_{\|\boldsymbol{\delta}_v\|_2\le\Delta}\tfrac12\|\mathcal{M}(W,\mathbf{k}_t)-(\mathbf{v}_t+\boldsymbol{\delta}_v)\|_2^2$; the inner max has closed form $\boldsymbol{\delta}_v^* = \Delta\,(\mathbf{v}_t - \mathcal{M})/\|\mathcal{M}-\mathbf{v}_t\|_2$, giving $L = \tfrac12\|r\|_2^2 + \Delta\|r\|_2 + \tfrac12\Delta^2$ with residual $r = \mathcal{M}(W,\mathbf{k}_t)-\mathbf{v}_t$, and update $W_t = W_{t-1} - \eta\,(r\,\mathbf{k}_t^\top + \Delta\, \frac{r}{\|r\|_2}\mathbf{k}_t^\top)$; $\Delta$ learnable.

=== 6. New retention gates (Section 5.2) ===
(a) f-divergence retention over a scaled probability simplex $\mathcal{W}=\{W: \|W\|_1 = c,\ W_{jl}\ge 0\}$ (boundedness = built-in numerical stability): with $D_t(W,W') = \sum_{jl} W'_{jl} f(W_{jl}/W'_{jl})$ and linearized loss, the update is $W_t = W_{t-1}\odot g(-\zeta_t - \eta_t\nabla\ell(W_{t-1};\mathbf{k}_t,\mathbf{v}_t))$ where $g = (f')^{-1}$ and $\zeta_t$ enforces $\|W_t\|_1=c$. KL special case ($f(\tau)=\tau\ln\tau$) plus Shannon-entropy GLOBAL retention $G_t(W)=\sum_{jl}W_{jl}\log W_{jl}$ gives, via KKT,
$$W_t \leftarrow c\,\mathrm{Softmax}\big((1-\lambda_t)\log(W_{t-1}) - \eta'_t\,\nabla\ell(W_{t-1};\mathbf{k}_t,\mathbf{v}_t)\big),\quad \lambda_t = \frac{1/\alpha_t}{1/\alpha_t + 1/\eta_t},\ \eta'_t = \frac{1}{1/\alpha_t+1/\eta_t}.$$
This is exponentiated-gradient / multiplicative-weights as a memory rule: the softmax keeps state entries positive and sum-normalized, so the state can never blow up -- retention by renormalization rather than decay.
(b) Elastic-net retention, Learning-Retaining form: global $G_t(W)=\tfrac{1}{2\beta}\|W\|_2^2 + \tfrac{1}{\alpha}\|W\|_1$, local $D_t = \tfrac12\|W-W_{t-1}\|_2^2$, giving
$$W_t = \mathcal{S}_{\gamma}(\lambda W_{t-1} - \zeta\,\nabla\ell(W_{t-1};\mathbf{k}_t,\mathbf{v}_t)),\quad \gamma = \tfrac{\eta\beta}{\alpha(\eta+\beta)},\ \lambda=\tfrac{\beta}{\beta+\eta},\ \zeta=\eta\lambda,$$
where $\mathcal{S}_\gamma(z) = \mathrm{sign}(z)\max\{0,|z|-\gamma\}$ is element-wise soft-thresholding. Interpretation: $\lambda\in(0,1)$ = SOFT forgetting (multiplicative decay, like a classical gate); the thresholding = HARD forgetting (small entries snap exactly to zero, freeing capacity). Smooth surrogate for backprop: $\mathcal{S}_\gamma(z) \approx |z|\arctan(z/\gamma)/(\pi/2)$.
(c) Elastic-net, FTRL form: $R_t = \tfrac{1}{\eta}\|W\|^2 + \tfrac{1}{\alpha}\|W\|_1$ gives a dual-accumulator rule $A_t = A_{t-1} - \eta\nabla\ell$, $W_t = \mathcal{S}_{\eta/\alpha}(A_t)$.
(d) General $L_q$ stability ($1<q\le 2$): $R(W) = \tfrac{1}{2\eta(q-1)}\|W\|_q^2$ yields (Shalev-Shwartz 2012, sec. 2.6) $A_t = A_{t-1} - \eta\nabla\ell(W_{i-1};\mathbf{k}_t,\mathbf{v}_t)$, $W_t = A_t / \|A_t\|_p^{\,p-2}$ with $p = q/(q-1)$ (dual norm). The memory keeps a raw gradient accumulator $A_t$ and exposes a norm-controlled view $W_t$.
(e) Bregman-divergence retention (mirror descent): pick strictly convex $f$, $F(W)=\sum_{jl}f(W_{jl})$, $D_t = F(W)-F(W')-\langle \nabla F(W'), W-W'\rangle$; update $W_t = g(-\eta\nabla\ell(W_{t-1}) + F'(W_{t-1}))$ with $g=(F')^{-1}$ applied element-wise. $f(\tau)=\tau^2/2$ recovers plain GD; choosing $f'=$ inverse sigmoid gives $W_t = \sigma(\ln\frac{W_{t-1}}{1-W_{t-1}} - \eta\nabla\ell)$, confining every state entry to $(0,1)$ -- retention-gate-as-nonlinearity, injecting expressivity into the recurrence itself.

=== 7. The three shipped models (Section 5.3) ===
All three share the memory architecture: a 2-layer MLP with expansion factor 4, GELU activation, residual connection and LayerNorm: $\mathcal{M}(x) = x + \mathrm{LN}(W_1\,\sigma(W_2 x))$. All use plain GD as the memory algorithm. All decouple the inner learning rate $\eta_t$ from the retention rate $\alpha_t$ (an independent gate parameter $\beta_t \in [0,1]^d$), and all gates/learning rates are channel-wise ($\eta_t, \delta_t, \alpha_t \in \mathbb{R}^d$) produced by low-rank projections (rank $k \approx 32$-$64$, following RWKV-7) to bound parameter cost.
- MONETA$(p,q)$: $\ell_p$ attentional bias + hybrid $\ell_q$-stability + $\ell_2$ retention. Recurrence:
$$A_t = \alpha_t A_{t-1} - \eta_t \nabla\ell_p(W_{t-1};\mathbf{k}_t,\mathbf{v}_t),\qquad W_t = \frac{A_t}{\|A_t\|_q^{\,q-2}},$$
with $\nabla\ell_p = p\,[\mathrm{Sign}(W\mathbf{k}_t-\mathbf{v}_t)\odot|W\mathbf{k}_t-\mathbf{v}_t|^{p-1}]\mathbf{k}_t^\top$. Shipped with $(p,q)=(3,4)$. Design rationale: $p=3$ sharpens attention to badly-recalled (surprising) tokens; the $\ell_q$ normalization keeps the exposed memory on a controlled-norm shell, a stronger stability mechanism than multiplicative decay alone.
- YAAD: Huber-mixture bias (form (iii) above) + Titans-style retention $\mathrm{Ret}_t = \tfrac{1}{2\theta_t}\|W-W_{t-1}\|_F^2 + \tfrac{1}{\beta_t}\|W\|_2^2$:
$$W_t = \alpha_t W_{t-1} - \begin{cases}\eta_t\nabla\ell_2(W_{t-1};\mathbf{k}_t,\mathbf{v}_t) & \|\mathcal{M}(\mathbf{k}_t)-\mathbf{v}_t\|\le\delta_t\\ \eta_t\,\delta_t\,\nabla\ell_1(W_{t-1};\mathbf{k}_t,\mathbf{v}_t) & \text{otherwise},\end{cases}$$
with input-dependent learned threshold $\delta_t$. Rationale: outlier tokens (noise, adversarial spans) should not be allowed to swing the memory by their full magnitude.
- MEMORA: plain $\ell_2$ bias + KL retention (Eq. 21 machinery):
$$W_t = \mathrm{Softmax}(\alpha_t \log(W_{t-1}) - \eta_t\nabla\ell_2(W_{t-1};\mathbf{k}_t,\mathbf{v}_t)).$$
Rationale: a simplex-constrained (softmax-renormalized) state is provably bounded -- forgetting emerges from probability-mass competition among entries rather than from decay, and the state cannot explode regardless of context length. (The same rule applies per-slice when $W$ is the MLP's weights.)

=== 8. Block architecture ===
Miras layers drop into the Llama macro-architecture in place of attention: SwiGLU MLP blocks, RoPE, RMSNorm. Each Miras token-mixing block: q/k/v linear projections, each followed by a depthwise-separable 1D conv (kernel 4); $\ell_2$ normalization on q and k (training stability); the memory readout is normalized and gated by a linear layer (output gate, following GSS/Mehta et al.). Hybrid variants (Moneta-H/Yaad-H/Memora-H) follow Samba: sequentially interleave Miras layers with Sliding-Window Attention layers.
outer_loop_training:
What is meta-learned (outer loop, standard pre-training with AdamW-style optimization on next-token loss): all projection matrices W_Q/W_K/W_V that manufacture keys/values/queries, the depthwise convs, output gates, RMSNorm/LN scales, the SwiGLU channel-mixing MLPs, the low-rank hypernetworks that emit the channel-wise inner-loop hyperparameters (learning rate eta_t, retention/decay gates alpha_t or beta_t, Huber threshold delta_t), and the INITIAL memory parameters. The inner-loop hyperparameters being input-dependent outputs of learned projections is the crucial coupling: the outer loop learns a policy for how aggressively the inner loop should write and retain, per token and per channel. Gradients flow through the inner loop by ordinary backpropagation through the unrolled memory-update recurrence -- every inner GD step W_t = alpha_t W_{t-1} - eta_t grad(...) is a differentiable function of (a) the token's k_t, v_t, (b) the emitted gates, and (c) the previous state, so d(loss)/d(outer params) traverses the whole chain. This is exactly why the paper insists on smooth surrogates: Sign(x) ~= tanh(alpha*x), |x| ~= sqrt(x^2 + eps) with eps = 1e-6 (for the Lp and L1/Huber gradients), and S_gamma(z) ~= |z| * arctan(z/gamma) / (pi/2) (for the soft-thresholding retention) -- the raw operators have zero or undefined derivatives and would kill or destabilize the outer gradient. [Background scaffolding needed for inference-only readers: the model is trained by 'backprop through an optimizer' -- the inner GD trace is part of the forward graph, so training cost and memory include the unrolled inner steps; this is the same trick as MAML-style meta-learning.]

Chunkwise-parallel training (the trick that makes this feasible on accelerators, following Titans and TTT): split the sequence into chunks of size b (16 or 64). Within a chunk, replace the exact per-token gradient grad l(M_{t-1}; k_t, v_t) by grad l(M_{t'}; k_t, v_t) where t' = t - mod(t, b) is the LAST state of the PREVIOUS chunk. All b gradients in a chunk then depend only on one frozen state and can be computed at once as dense matmuls; the intra-chunk recurrence becomes linear (a cumulative gated sum). Expanding the recurrence: M_t = beta_t * M_0 - sum_{i=1..t} (beta_t / beta_i) * eta_i * grad l(M_{t'}; k_i, v_i), with beta_i = prod_{j<=i} alpha_j (cumulative decay products). For the Lp loss the whole-chunk gradient sum collapses to p * E_b (.) B_b (.) Sign(W_0 K - V) (.) |W_0 K - V|^{p-1} K^T, where K, V stack the chunk's keys/values, E_b = diag-broadcast of the eta_i, and B_b broadcasts the decay ratios beta_b / beta_i -- i.e., one batched matmul plus elementwise ops. Nonlinearities that would break linearity are hoisted to chunk boundaries only: Moneta's Lq-normalization W_t = A_t / ||A_t||_q^{q-2} is applied at the end of each chunk, not per token; Yaad computes BOTH the l1 and l2 chunk gradients and combines them with a mask I(||M(k_t) - v_t|| <= delta_t); Memora is the hard case because log and Softmax at the same chunk boundary would cancel (softmax(log(x) - g) collapses the log), so the paper introduces a LAG TOKEN: at the first token of each chunk (index i = k*b + 1) one genuine nonlinear step M_1 = Softmax(alpha_1 log(M_0) - eta_1 grad l2(M_0; k_1, v_1)) is taken, and the rest of the chunk runs linearly from M_1. This means the trained model is an APPROXIMATION of the per-token math: gradients are computed against a slightly stale state (up to b-1 tokens old) and state nonlinearities fire once per chunk. The paper does not quantify the approximation error; it inherits the empirical justification from Titans/TTT.

Outer-loop experimental config (Appendix C, Table 5): 170M (12 blocks, dim 768, 16 heads, peak LR 3e-3, 15B tokens), 340M (24 blocks, dim 1024, 16 heads, 1.5e-3, 15B), 780M (24 blocks, dim 1536, 16 heads, 1.25e-3, 30B); training context window 4096; FineWeb-Edu for LM/reasoning runs, C4 for scaling-law runs.
inner_loop_test_time:
What changes during inference: per Miras layer (and per head), the fast weights of a 2-layer MLP memory M(x) = x + LN(W1 sigma(W2 x)) with expansion 4 -- i.e., W1 in R^{d x 4d} and W2 in R^{4d x d}, roughly 8*d^2 scalars of mutable state per head-layer, PLUS, for Moneta, a second accumulator A_t of the same shape (the FTRL dual variable), effectively doubling mutable state to ~16*d^2; Yaad and Memora keep a single copy. Everything else (projections, convs, gates' hypernetworks, channel-mixing MLPs) is frozen at inference. The update rule per token is one smoothed gradient-descent step on the layer's attentional bias, with channel-wise data-dependent learning rate eta_t, retention gate alpha_t, and (Yaad) threshold delta_t, all emitted by frozen low-rank projections from the current token:
- Moneta: A_t = alpha_t A_{t-1} - eta_t * p * [tanh-smoothed Sign(residual) (.) |residual|^{p-1}] backpropped through the memory MLP; W_t = A_t / ||A_t||_q^{q-2}, with (p, q) = (3, 4).
- Yaad: compute residual norm; if <= delta_t take an l2 gradient step, else a delta_t-scaled l1 (sign) gradient step; then multiply by retention alpha_t (Titans-style gate, no momentum).
- Memora: W_t = Softmax(alpha_t log W_{t-1} - eta_t grad_l2), an exponentiated-gradient step keeping state entries positive and normalized.
Per-token compute: one forward pass through the memory MLP to form the prediction M(k_t) (~2 * 8d^2 = 16d^2 MACs), one backward pass through the 2-layer MLP to get gradients w.r.t. W1, W2 (~2x forward, ~32d^2 MACs), plus the elementwise retention/normalization update over the ~8d^2 state entries (Memora adds an elementwise log + exp + a global sum for softmax normalization over the state; Moneta adds a q-norm reduction). Then one more forward pass with the query to READ the memory output y_t = M(q_t). Order of magnitude: ~50-60 d^2 MACs per token per head-layer, a constant independent of context length -- versus attention's per-token cost growing as N*d with the KV cache. At serving time the practical implementation can also use the same chunkwise prefill (process the prompt in chunks of b with batched matmuls, states materialized at chunk boundaries) and fall back to strict per-token recurrence at decode. Memory traffic, not FLOPs, is the binding constraint at decode: each token must read AND write the full ~8d^2 (or 16d^2) state, whereas a matrix-memory model like Gated DeltaNet moves only d^2. Note the optimizer here is deliberately the simplest in the family: plain GD, no momentum (unlike Titans-LMM) -- the expressivity is moved into the objective and the retention gate instead.

concepts_introduced.name: Attentional bias (as internal objective)
concepts_introduced.definition: The internal loss L(M(K); V) that an associative-memory sequence layer minimizes online over keys/values; formalizes 'what the model prioritizes memorizing'. The paper's central coinage: every sequence model is characterized by its attentional bias.

concepts_introduced.name: Retention gate
concepts_introduced.definition: Re-naming and generalization of the forget gate: the regularization term Ret_t(W, W_{t-1}) = D_t(W, W_{t-1})/eta_t + G_t(W)/alpha_t that balances learning new pairs against retaining the previous state. Classical gates = L2/Frobenius special cases; new choices include KL/f-divergence, elastic net, Lq, Bregman.

concepts_introduced.name: Miras framework
concepts_introduced.definition: Design space for sequence models as the 4-tuple (memory architecture, attentional bias, retention gate, memory learning algorithm); claims to uniquely situate Transformers, all linear RNNs, TTT, and Titans (Table 1).

concepts_introduced.name: Learning-Retaining viewpoint
concepts_introduced.definition: Per-step proximal view: W_t = argmin_W [approx loss on newest pair + Ret_t(W, W_{t-1})]. Proven (Prop 3.2) to subsume the FTRL viewpoint via Bregman-divergence retention; the paper's preferred derivation lens.

concepts_introduced.name: FTRL viewpoint
concepts_introduced.definition: Follow-The-Regularized-Leader view: W_t = argmin_W [sum of linearized losses over ALL past tokens + R_t(W)/eta_t]; explains dual-accumulator update rules (Moneta's A_t).

concepts_introduced.name: Local vs. global retention
concepts_introduced.definition: Decomposition of retention into D_t(W, W_{t-1}) (stay near previous state; premetric) and G_t(W) (bound the memory's size); eta_t acting as a 'meta in-context learning rate'.

concepts_introduced.name: Value-less associative memory
concepts_introduced.definition: The p=1 instance of the Lp bias: the memory stores keys but maps them only to {-1, +1} via sign updates; interpreted as a coping mechanism for extreme events.

concepts_introduced.name: Moneta
concepts_introduced.definition: Miras variant: 2-layer MLP memory, Lp attentional bias (p=3), hybrid Lq-stability retention (q=4) with dual accumulator A_t and normalized exposed memory W_t = A_t/||A_t||_q^{q-2}, plain GD.

concepts_introduced.name: Yaad
concepts_introduced.definition: Miras variant: 2-layer MLP memory, Huber-mixture attentional bias with learned input-dependent threshold delta_t (l2 step for inliers, delta-scaled l1 step for outliers), Titans-style L2 retention, plain GD.

concepts_introduced.name: Memora
concepts_introduced.definition: Miras variant: 2-layer MLP memory, l2 attentional bias, KL-divergence retention over a scaled probability simplex, giving the exponentiated-gradient/softmax update W_t = Softmax(alpha_t log W_{t-1} - eta_t grad); guaranteed-bounded state.

concepts_introduced.name: Hard vs. soft forgetting
concepts_introduced.definition: From the elastic-net retention gate: soft = multiplicative shrinkage by lambda in (0,1) (classical gating); hard = soft-thresholding S_gamma snapping small state entries exactly to zero, freeing capacity.

concepts_introduced.name: Lag token (chunk-boundary nonlinear step)
concepts_introduced.definition: Training trick for Memora: apply the full nonlinear softmax-log update only at the first token of each chunk (i = k*b+1) so the log is not cancelled by the boundary softmax, and run linearized updates inside the chunk.

concepts_introduced.name: Retention-as-renormalization
concepts_introduced.definition: Implicit concept: constraining the state to a simplex/ball (Memora, Lq) makes forgetting emerge from normalization/competition rather than decay -- a qualitatively different stability mechanism than gated exponential decay.

assumptions_and_scope: Scope: autoregressive language modeling with fixed-size-state recurrent layers; models up to 1.3B params / 100B tokens; training context 4K (scaling study to 32K); English web corpora (FineWeb-Edu, C4). The unification claims hold at the level of the ORIGINAL design equations of each model (Table 1 caveat: architectural choices don't uniquely identify a backbone -- input-dependency, channel-wise parameterization, convs, and hybrid attention are orthogonal 'minor' axes, and the L2-retention column lumps together 'L2-like' gates that differ in detail; strictly only Titans and RWKV-7 use the exact L2 retention as derived). Key derivations assume linearized losses (local linear approximation of l at W_{t-1}) and, for closed forms, matrix memory M(W,k) = W k; the MLP-memory versions apply the same rules per-parameter-slice without new theory. Proposition 3.2 (Learning-Retaining generalizes FTRL) requires constant eta, unconstrained W = R^d, and strict convexity of the accumulated objective h_t -- none of which hold exactly for the deep-memory, gated, constrained instantiations actually shipped; the equivalence is a motivation, not a guarantee. The chunkwise-parallel training computes gradients against a stale (up to b-1 tokens old) state and defers state nonlinearities to chunk boundaries -- so the deployed models are trained on an approximation of their own per-token recurrence, with no error analysis given. Non-differentiable operators (Sign, |.|, soft-threshold) are replaced by smooth surrogates during outer training. No theory of memory capacity, regret bounds, or state-tracking expressivity is provided for the new variants; the justification is empirical. Efficiency claims are FLOPs- and design-level: no wall-clock throughput, kernel benchmarks, or latency measurements appear in the paper.
experiments_and_scale: Scales: 120M/170M, 340M (15B tokens), 760M/780M (30B tokens), 1.3B (100B tokens); training context 4096; FineWeb-Edu for LM + commonsense, C4 for scaling curves; baselines (numbers inherited from the Titans paper) = Transformer++, RetNet, GLA, Mamba, Mamba2, DeltaNet, TTT, Gated DeltaNet, plus hybrids Samba and Gated DeltaNet-H2. Benchmarks: WikiText ppl, LAMBADA ppl/acc, PIQA, HellaSwag, WinoGrande, ARC-e/ARC-c, SIQA, BoolQ; RULER Single-NIAH (S-NIAH-PK/N/W at 1K-8K). Headline numbers: at 340M/15B, Moneta reaches 26.19 Wiki ppl vs Gated DeltaNet 27.01, TTT 27.44, Transformer++ 31.52. At 760M/30B, Yaad 20.99 / Moneta 21.18 Wiki ppl vs Gated DeltaNet 21.18, Samba 20.63, GDN-H2 19.88; the hybrid Miras variants (Samba-style + SWA) push to Memora-H 18.24 / Yaad-H 18.59 / Moneta-H 18.72. At 1.3B/100B, pure-recurrent Yaad hits 15.18 and Moneta 15.52 Wiki ppl, beating not only Gated DeltaNet (16.42) but also the HYBRIDS Samba (16.13) and Gated DeltaNet-H2 (15.91) -- the paper's flagship claim that attention-free models with better attentional bias + retention beat attention hybrids. S-NIAH averages: Moneta 93.5, Yaad 92.9, Memora 92.1 vs Gated DeltaNet 75.8, TTT 66.1, DeltaNet 57.9, Mamba2 52.0; Moneta is strongest on the synthetic-noise variant S-NIAH-PK (98.8 at 8K), credited to the noise-robust p-norm objective. Scaling: all three variants show better ppl-vs-FLOPs and better ppl-vs-context-length (2K to 32K, at 340M and 760M) than baselines. Ablations: sweeping p in {1, 1.5, 2, 2.8, 3, 3.2, 4} is NON-monotone -- best p = 3, worst p = 4 -- and p does not change the context-length scaling shape, whereas sweeping q in {2, 3, 4, 5} DOES change the scaling pattern (retention gate quality governs long-context behavior). Yaad component ablation (Avg LM score 53.98): removing the retention gate costs -3.35 (50.63); making delta input-independent costs -1.79; dropping the l2 branch -1.12; dropping the l1 branch -0.94; replacing the MLP memory with a linear one -2.41.
systems_implications: State size: each Miras layer's recurrent state is a full 2-layer MLP (expansion 4) per head: W1 (d x 4d) + W2 (4d x d) = 8 d^2 parameters of fp state per head per layer -- 8x a DeltaNet/GDN matrix state (d^2) and vastly more than Mamba2's; Moneta doubles this with its accumulator A_t (~16 d^2). Concretely, with head dim 64: 32K state entries per head (Moneta 64K) vs 4K for a matrix state. The break-even against a KV cache (2 * N * d per head for K+V) is at N ~= 4d tokens (~256 tokens at d=64), so for any long context the state is dramatically smaller than a KV cache and CONSTANT in N -- the standard linear-RNN serving win (O(1) memory and per-token FLOPs at decode, no cache paging), but with an 8-16x fatter state than prior linear RNNs, which matters for batched serving: state residency per sequence, state checkpointing for prefix caching, and beam/speculative branching all cost 8-16x more than GDN. Per-token decode work = forward + backward + read through the memory MLP (~50-60 d^2 MACs/head-layer) -- roughly 3-4x a GDN-style update -- and is memory-bandwidth-bound: the whole state is read and rewritten every token. Training/prefill: chunkwise-parallel formulation (chunk b = 16 or 64) turns the inner loop into dense batched matmuls (Sign/abs/elementwise ops fused around a |W0 K - V|^{p-1} K^T GEMM) with sequential dependence only ACROSS chunks -- same kernel skeleton as Titans/TTT/GLA-style chunkwise kernels, so N/b sequential steps of O(b^2 + b d^2)-ish work; state nonlinearities (Moneta's q-norm normalization, Memora's log/softmax lag-token step) execute only once per chunk boundary, keeping them off the critical inner path. Distinctive kernel considerations: (1) Moneta's ||A_t||_q reduction is a global norm over 8 d^2 entries per boundary -- a reduction kernel between GEMM phases; (2) Memora's softmax over the ENTIRE state (not over tokens) requires a stable log-sum-exp over 8 d^2 entries and keeps state strictly positive -- friendly to low-precision storage in principle (bounded, normalized), though the log amplifies small-value quantization error; (3) Yaad needs dual gradient computation (l1 and l2 branches) plus a mask -- ~2x elementwise work, one extra residual-norm reduction per token; (4) smooth surrogates (tanh, sqrt(x^2+eps), arctan-thresholding) are cheap elementwise epilogues. Channel-wise gates via rank-32/64 hypernetworks add negligible FLOPs/params. The paper reports NO wall-clock numbers, no kernel implementation details, and no decode-throughput comparison -- FLOPs-matched perplexity (Figure 3 left) is the only efficiency evidence; an infra reader should treat 'fast parallelizable training' as an asymptotic/structural claim inherited from the Titans/TTT chunkwise recipe. Hybrids (Samba-style Miras + SWA interleave) reintroduce a small sliding-window KV cache (window-sized, O(w d)) on top of the recurrent state.
connections: Backward lineage, within the study set: this paper is the direct theoretical sequel to Titans (2501.00663, same lead author) -- Titans-LMM appears in Table 1 as one row of Miras (nonlinear L2 bias, local+global L2 retention, GD+momentum), and Miras generalizes Titans' 'surprise metric' (the gradient of the inner objective) and its forget gate (the L2 global retention with cold-start, footnote 2 explicitly contrasts Titans' gating with Mamba2/GDN full-erase gating). It supplies the vocabulary (attentional bias, retention gate, four-axis design space) that the later papers in this set inhabit: ATLAS (2505.23735) varies the memory-algorithm and objective axes (sliding-window/Omega-style objectives over multiple tokens, Muon-type second-order-ish inner optimizers) on exactly this scaffold, and the subsequent nested/continual-learning papers (2511.07343, 2512.24695, 2606.03979) extend the same inner-objective view to deeper optimizer nesting; Miras is the taxonomy those papers assume. External lineage it builds on and subsumes: fast weight programmers (Schmidhuber 1992/93; Schlag et al. 2021 'linear transformers are secretly FWPs') supply the fast-weight-as-memory idea and the Hebbian/delta dichotomy Miras formalizes as dot-product vs L2 attentional bias; linear attention (Katharopoulos 2020), RetNet, GLA, Mamba/Mamba2, HGRN2 are recovered as gated-Hebbian instances; DeltaNet (via Yang et al.'s parallelized delta rule) and Gated DeltaNet / RWKV-7 / DeltaProduct as L2-bias GD instances with scalar/channel-wise/multi-step variations; Longhorn is singled out as IMPLICIT (proximal) GD on the same objective; TTT-Linear/TTT-MLP (Sun et al. 2024) contribute both the deep-memory-as-inner-learner view and the parametric-vs-nonparametric reading of linear vs softmax attention that Miras adopts for its attention row; Mesa-layer (von Oswald et al.) is the Newton's-method row. The retention-gate section imports classical optimization machinery wholesale: FTRL and mirror descent (Shalev-Shwartz, Hazan), Bregman divergences, elastic net (LASSO+Ridge), f-divergences/KL, exponentiated gradient. Against the concurrent unifier Wang et al. 2025 ('test-time regression'), the appendix argues Miras is strictly finer-grained: Wang et al. must approximate RetNet/Mamba as regression solvers, collapsing the Hebbian/delta distinction, and cannot express HGRN2, Moneta, Yaad, or Memora at all. What it leaves open: no wall-clock or kernel story; the memory-ALGORITHM axis is deliberately under-explored (all three shipped models use plain GD -- no momentum, no second-order, no multi-step; the paper explicitly points to Newton/other optimizers as future work, which is precisely the axis ATLAS then takes); per-token single-pair objectives only (no multi-token/window inner objectives -- also ATLAS's opening); no theory (capacity, regret, state-tracking class) for the new biases/gates; and the chunkwise approximation error is unquantified.
open_questions: (1) Approximation fidelity: how much does the chunkwise stale-gradient trick (gradients w.r.t. the previous chunk's last state, nonlinearities only at boundaries, Memora's lag-token) change the model relative to its per-token definition, and does the gap grow with chunk size b or context length? No error analysis or b-ablation is given. (2) The memory-algorithm axis is left almost untouched: all shipped variants use plain GD; would momentum (Titans), implicit/proximal steps (Longhorn), multi-step (DeltaProduct), or quasi-Newton inner optimizers compose with the new biases/gates? (This is exactly the question ATLAS answers next.) (3) Why (p,q) = (3,4)? The p-sweep is non-monotone with best p=3 and worst p=4, and q qualitatively changes context scaling -- but there is no theory linking p/q to data statistics, and per-task or learned/adaptive p is untried. (4) Serving economics: 8-16x larger recurrent state and 3-4x per-token update cost vs matrix-state models -- is the quality gain worth it at production batch sizes, and can the state be quantized/sparsified (the elastic-net hard-forgetting gate hints at exploitable state sparsity but is not shipped in any of the three models)? (5) Memora's simplex constraint on MLP weights: what does a positive, sum-normalized weight matrix do to the memory's representational capacity, and does per-slice normalization interact badly with the residual/LayerNorm memory architecture? (6) No regret bounds, capacity results, or state-tracking (e.g., TC0 vs NC1) analysis for any new variant, despite the framework importing the entire online-convex-optimization toolkit whose guarantees require convexity the 2-layer-MLP memory breaks. (7) Retrieval beyond single-needle: S-NIAH is the only long-context recall test; multi-needle, multi-hop, and extrapolation far beyond 32K are unexplored. (8) The claim that pure-recurrent Miras beats hybrids at 1.3B invites the obvious follow-up -- does that ordering survive at 7B+ scale and on tasks where exact-copy recall dominates?
